vignette:
He is seventy-five now, a quiet Latin American man who still introduces himself first through his work. Even after retirement age, he continues part-time as a QA engineer, consulting from home on software testing projects because, as he says, he has always trusted systems more when he can check them himself. He speaks carefully, in ordered sequences, and when he tells the story of the disaster, he tries at first to do the same-starting with the weather reports, the small warning signs, the things that should have been enough.

Years ago, he and his wife were living in a coastal city when the storm came. He remembers the air changing before anything else: a pressure in his ears, a strange stillness, then the radio announcer's voice growing sharper. He spent the day doing what he knew how to do-verifying, comparing, preparing. He checked battery levels in flashlights, labeled medication bottles, filled containers with water, tested the portable radio twice. His wife told him to sit down and rest, but he kept moving from room to room, unsettled by the sense that he had missed something important.

By evening the rain had become violent, thrown against the windows in hard sheets. Then the power failed. He remembers the sudden dark as something alive. The house began to shake under the wind. Water pushed in under the door, then faster than he thought possible. In his memory, events become fragmented here: his wife shouting over the storm, furniture scraping, the smell of wet wood and sewage, the sound of glass breaking somewhere behind him. He can still see the beam of his flashlight jerking wildly over the walls as he tried to guide them to higher ground inside the house. At one point he lost hold of his wife's hand for only a moment, but that moment remains enormous in his mind. He says it felt like the world had opened and taken away all the rules he had counted on.

They survived by climbing into a cramped upper storage space and waiting through the night while the house groaned around them. He recalls listening for collapsing walls and for his wife's breathing, counting the seconds between gusts, promising himself that if he stayed alert enough, vigilant enough, he could keep disaster from becoming death. By morning the neighborhood was unrecognizable-mud, broken roofs, overturned cars, people calling out names into the wet gray air. He helped a neighbor move debris with trembling hands and later realized he could not feel his fingers.

In the months afterward, everyone talked about rebuilding. He tried to join in that language of progress and gratitude. He returned to work eventually, first in person, later remotely, and told himself that structure would repair him. But storms, even mild ones, began to undo him. The first time heavy rain hit the office windows, his chest tightened so quickly he thought he was having a heart attack. He went to the restroom and locked himself in a stall, ashamed, pressing his palms against his knees until the shaking passed. At home he started checking weather forecasts obsessively, then checking backup batteries, flashlights, chargers, window latches, bottled water. His wife would wake in the night and find him standing in the hallway listening for sounds outside.

He does not describe nightmares immediately, but they are there. In them he is back in the dark house, searching for his wife with a flashlight that will not stay on. Sometimes he wakes calling her name. More often he wakes before dawn, soaked in sweat, already alert, his body convinced something terrible is beginning again. On those mornings he cannot return to sleep. He paces, makes coffee too early, opens multiple weather apps, and watches the sky through the kitchen window. His wife tells him the morning is calm. He nods, but his body does not believe her.

Over time he narrows his life without quite meaning to. He avoids family gatherings if rain is predicted. He refuses invitations to visit relatives in coastal areas. During hurricane season he becomes irritable and distracted, his attention pulled away from conversation toward contingency plans. In his QA work, his old strengths become sharper and more rigid. He rechecks test cases long after they are complete, unable to tolerate uncertainty. If a system alert sounds on his computer, even an ordinary notification, he startles visibly. He laughs it off in meetings, but afterward he feels embarrassed and exhausted.

What troubles him most is not fear alone but the feeling that the storm never fully ended. He says he knows, rationally, that he is in his own home, in a different place, decades older. Yet when rain hits the roof at night, his thoughts collapse into the old logic: prepare, monitor, don't sleep too deeply, keep watch. He becomes distant with his wife at those times, not because he does not love her, but because loving her makes him feel again how close he came to losing her. He carries guilt that he could not protect her better, though she reminds him they survived together.

In session, he often catches himself apologizing for being "dramatic." Then he describes sitting in his living room during an ordinary thunderstorm, television muted, hands clasped so tightly they ache, waiting for catastrophe with the same grim concentration he once brought to debugging software. He is a man who built a life on detecting failures before they spread. Since the storm, his mind keeps scanning for the next breach, as if vigilance alone might hold back the water.
